title: Where Does Hamas Stand Three Years After Oct. 7 – and What Comes Next?
author: Muhammad Shehada
content:

Three years after Hamas launched its deadliest attack on Israel, the group
finds itself in perhaps its worst predicament since its inception. The
movement that has built its identity and purpose around armed resistance has
come to realize that its weapons in Gaza won't move the needle, but it can't
find a viable alternative to coalesce around.

Despite Israel killing [more than 1,450
Palestinians](https://t.me/s/MOHMediaGaza) since the Trump-brokered ceasefire
of October 2025 went into effect, including many of Hamas's top militant
commanders, its militants [haven't fired a single bullet or
rocket](https://arabcenterdc.org/resource/hamas-and-the-politics-of-
decommissioning-in-gaza/) at Israel or its military in retaliation (Hamas has
denied Israel's accusations that the group has violated the ceasefire). In
July, Hamas begrudgingly agreed to lay down its arms in Gaza in return for
Israeli withdrawal. The group's leaders even ceased their fiery speeches,
rhetorical threats, and public spectacles of strength. Their latest statements
focus more on survival than liberation. Hamas is now [divided
between](https://www.ynet.co.il/news/article/bkpkz3ovfg) those who call
October 7 a "[disaster](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c90l_Y7tGW4)" and a
"strategic mistake," and those who feel compelled to use Yahya Sinwar's legacy
to maintain popularity and legitimacy among the movement's supporters.

How did Hamas get here? Where does the movement stand today? And what comes
next?
